title: Erdős Problem #226: Entire Functions Preserving Rationality
description: Is there an entire non-linear function f such that x ∈ ℚ ↔ f(x) ∈ ℚ for all real x? SOLVED: YES by Barth-Schneider (1970). For any two countable dense sets A, B ⊂ ℝ, a transcendental entire function mapping A to B exists.

overview.historicalContext: The question of arithmetic control over analytic functions dates to Stäckel (1895), who showed a transcendental entire function can take rational values at all rationals — but his construction did not control irrational inputs. Erdős sharpened this to an $\textit{if and only if}$ question: can $f(x) \in \mathbb{Q} \Leftrightarrow x \in \mathbb{Q}$? Hayman included it as Problem 2.31 in his 1974 collection, attributing it to Erdős. Barth and Schneider solved it affirmatively in 1970, proving the much stronger result that for ANY countable dense $A, B \subset \mathbb{R}$, a transcendental entire $f$ with $f(A) = B$ exists — and can be made strictly monotone on $\mathbb{R}$. Their 1971 follow-up extended this to countable dense subsets of $\mathbb{C}$. The construction uses Weierstrass products and careful interpolation on the countable dense set.
overview.problemStatement: Is there an entire non-linear function f : ℂ → ℂ such that for all x ∈ ℝ, x ∈ ℚ ↔ f(x) ∈ ℚ? More generally, for any countable dense A, B ⊆ ℝ, does an entire function with f(A) = B exist? SOLVED: YES (Barth-Schneider, 1970).
overview.text: Is there an entire non-linear function f such that x ∈ ℚ ↔ f(x) ∈ ℚ for all real x? SOLVED: YES by Barth-Schneider (1970). For any two countable dense sets A, B ⊂ ℝ, a transcendental entire function mapping A to B exists.
overview.proofStrategy: The formalization axiomatizes the Barth-Schneider existence theorem and derives both the original and generalized answers. The key proof step in `erdos_question_affirmative` instantiates the axiom with $A = B = \mathbb{Q}$ (via `rationals_countable_dense`), then shows transcendental $\Rightarrow$ non-linear by encoding any linear function $f(z) = az + b$ as a degree-1 polynomial, contradicting transcendence. The `general_question_affirmative` follows directly. The formalization also axiomatizes the $\mathbb{C}$ extension and the impossibility of polynomial solutions.
keyInsights: The function must be transcendental — no polynomial can preserve rationality while being non-linear
The function can be made strictly monotone on ℝ
Result holds for ANY pair of countable dense sets, not just ℚ
The theorem extends to countable dense subsets of ℂ (1971)
Construction uses Weierstrass products and interpolation
prerequisites: Topology (countable dense subsets of ℝ and ℂ)
Algebraic number theory (rationality of polynomial values)

conclusion.summary: Erdős Problem #226 was SOLVED by Barth and Schneider (1970). An entire non-linear function preserving rationality exists. More generally, for any countable dense sets A, B ⊂ ℝ, a transcendental entire function maps A to B. The result extends to ℂ.
conclusion.implications:
**Theoretical Significance**: The solution reveals surprising flexibility in transcendental entire functions: they can precisely control which points map to which among countable dense sets, while being holomorphic everywhere.

This connects complex analysis (Weierstrass products, Runge's theorem) to the arithmetic structure of dense subsets. The monotonicity result is especially striking — the function respects the order structure of $\mathbb{R}$ while performing this arithmetic rearrangement.
openQuestions: Can the growth rate of the constructed Barth-Schneider function be controlled (e.g., can it have finite order)?
What is the smallest order of growth needed for rationality-preserving entire functions?
Can similar results be obtained for the algebraic numbers $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ instead of $\mathbb{Q}$?
Is there a constructive or computable version of the Barth-Schneider result?

crossReferences.description: Both address arithmetic structure in analytic settings — Dirichlet's theorem controls primes in arithmetic progressions, Barth-Schneider controls rational values of entire functions

Both involve the boundary between algebraic and transcendental: Abel-Ruffini shows polynomial roots can be non-algebraic in radicals, while Problem 226 shows only transcendental functions can biject rationals
